tool_signatures.name: arkime_connections
tool_signatures.description: Build a source/destination connection graph of who talked to whom.

src_field.description: Arkime db field for source nodes (default srcIp). Common choices: srcIp, dstIp, dstPort, node — arkime_field_search's db column. The dotted storage path works here too and gives the identical graph: srcIp/dstIp and source.ip/destination.ip draw the same nodes and links. What this route will NOT take is the exp column: srcField=ip.src gets HTTP 403 and dstField=port.dst HTTP 500 "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined", so the expression names whose db spelling differs are refused here before the request is sent.

dst_field.description: Arkime db field for destination nodes (default dstIp; dstPort graphs by port instead of by host). Same vocabulary as src_field: db column or dotted storage path, never the exp column.

expression.description: Optional Arkime expression syntax to scope the graph. Empty = all sessions.

sessions.description: How many matching sessions the graph is drawn from (Arkime's length; its own default is 100). More sessions find more hosts and take longer: on Malcolm's training instance a query matching 41,768 sessions drew 8 nodes from 100 sessions, 23 from 10,000 (1.4 s) and 39 from 50,000 (3.5 s).

time_from.description: Start time as EPOCH SECONDS (NOT a dateparser string). Empty = Arkime's recent-only default.

time_to.description: End time as EPOCH SECONDS (NOT a dateparser string). Empty = now.

tool_signatures.name: arkime_session_payload
tool_signatures.description: Read the decoded payload of one Arkime session — the bytes that crossed the wire.

session_id.description: One Arkime session id from arkime_sessions results, in either spelling: the bare id or the node-prefixed "3@231115:231115-..." form (both reach the same session). arkime_sessions is the only source of these ids.

node.description: Capture node that recorded the session — the `node` field of the arkime_sessions row. Leave empty and it is looked up from the session document, at the cost of one extra request. A name this deployment does not have is reported as an input error rather than answered, because Arkime replies 200 to it.

base.description: How to render the bytes: "hex" for an offset + hex + ASCII gutter (what makes a binary protocol such as Modbus legible), "ascii" or "utf8" for text protocols such as HTTP. Anything else is rejected here — Arkime would silently fall back to ASCII.

packets.description: How many packets to decode, counted as packets and not as rendered blocks: consecutive same-direction packets coalesce into one block and a packet with no payload renders nothing, so a TCP session opening with a handshake can spend the first few on column headers alone. Raise it to read further into the conversation, a few at a time: what each packet costs scales with the bytes it carried, so the same value can render a few hundred characters on one session and tens of thousands on another. The 200,000-character cap is the backstop.

tool_signatures.name: arkime_sessions
tool_signatures.description: Search Arkime sessions by expression; returns trimmed rows each carrying a session id.

expression.description: Arkime expression syntax (NOT OpenSearch DSL, NOT a Malcolm filter dict). Examples: "ip==192.0.2.77"; "ip.src==192.0.2.77 && ip.dst==198.51.100.1"; "protocols==dns"; "port.dst==443"; "http.uri==/login*"; "country.dst==CN". Every clause must be field-operator-value — there is no free-text search. Field existence is the literal token EXISTS!, as in "zeek.ftp.password == EXISTS!". A list is an OR: "port == [80,443]". Field names are Arkime's own, NOT the ECS names malcolm_field_search returns — look them up with arkime_field_search. A name Arkime cannot resolve, or an expression it cannot parse, is reported as an error carrying Arkime's own message.

limit.description: Max sessions to return. Each row is a JSON object carrying its own keys, which is why this stops at 100; when you want thousands of rows and no session id, arkime_sessions_csv takes up to 10,000.

time_from.description: Start time as EPOCH SECONDS (NOT a dateparser string like "7 days ago"). Empty = Arkime's recent-only default; pass a range for historical data.

time_to.description: End time as EPOCH SECONDS (NOT a dateparser string). Empty = now.
